name: Chromium picolinate

card.summary: Chromium supplement sold to curb cravings and cut fat; reviews report no reliable evidence of weight or muscle effects.
card.note: Rare case reports of kidney and liver injury at high intakes; may interact with diabetes medicines.

quick.overview:
Chromium picolinate is a form of trivalent chromium bound to picolinic acid, sold as a supplement for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar support. Forum interest centres on claims that it reduces carbohydrate cravings.

A 2013 Cochrane review, as summarised by Wikipedia, found no reliable evidence to draw firm conclusions on weight loss or muscle gain in overweight adults. The European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence for a body-weight effect.
quick.mechanism: Chromium is proposed to enhance insulin signalling, sometimes through a peptide called chromodulin. Wikipedia reports that the insulin-receptor effects were seen in vitro but not adequately shown in living organisms, and the exact mechanism is unknown.
quick.risks: Typical supplement amounts show little evidence of toxicity. Reported effects include allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and irritability, and rare case reports describe kidney or liver injury at high intakes. It may interact with insulin and other drugs. Regulators have approved only a heavily qualified US health claim about insulin resistance.

lead: Chromium(III) picolinate is a pink-red coordination compound of trivalent chromium and picolinic acid, sold as a dietary supplement and marketed in the United States to athletes for muscle development and for weight loss. [2]

Whether chromium is an essential nutrient is debated; the European Food Safety Authority found no convincing evidence to justify intake recommendations. [2] Reviews of supplementation report either no effect on muscle or fat or a small weight loss in trials longer than 12 weeks, and a 2013 Cochrane review found no reliable evidence for firm conclusions. [2] A 2004 systematic review of dietary supplements for body-weight reduction also examined such products. [3]
In 2005 the US FDA allowed only a qualified health claim describing a relationship to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk as highly uncertain. [2]
infobox: Dietary supplement (US); qualified FDA health claim (2005)

paras: The compound has a distorted octahedral geometry with three picolinate ligands. It is poorly soluble in water and was first reported in 1917; its crystal structure was described in 2013. [2]

A 2000 review described a proposed role for the oligopeptide chromodulin, which binds chromium in response to insulin and may amplify insulin-receptor signalling. [4] Wikipedia notes that this has not been adequately shown in vivo and that the biological mechanism remains undetermined. [2] Absorption is low, about 2 percent, but higher than inorganic chromium. [2]

A 1997 trial of 180 people with type 2 diabetes reported improved glucose and insulin variables with higher chromium intakes. [5] A 2006 trial in people with type 2 diabetes reported that chromium picolinate attenuated weight gain and increased insulin sensitivity. [6] Rat studies in obese and diabetic models reported improvements in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism. [7][8]
Wikipedia says reviews found no association of supplementation with glucose or insulin levels and that it does not prevent or treat obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. [2]

Wikipedia reports intakes up to 1,000 micrograms daily considered safe, with reported allergic reactions, headache, insomnia, irritability and possible drug interactions. Case reports describe kidney failure at 600 micrograms per day for six weeks and liver disease at 1,200 to 2,400 micrograms per day. People using insulin and those pregnant or breastfeeding are advised to avoid it. [2]

Laboratory research on toxicity differs by chromium form: hexavalent chromium is an industrial toxin and carcinogen, whereas trivalent chromium is the supplement form. [9] In 2004 the UK Food Standards Agency advised consumers to avoid chromium picolinate over genotoxicity concerns, and withdrew that advice in December 2004 after the Committee on Mutagenicity found it was not mutagenic in vitro. [2]

In 2005 the FDA approved a qualified claim on insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk using wording that calls the relationship highly uncertain, and rejected other proposed claims; Health Canada approved supplement use with specified labelling in 2010. [2] A US homeopathic product label lists chromium picolinate among ingredients with the statement that claims are based on traditional homeopathic practice and not FDA evaluated. [10]

Registered human trials include chromium picolinate for food intake in obesity with atypical depression (n=42) [11], binge eating disorder (n=26) [12], metabolic syndrome (n=60) [13] and insulin resistance in obesity (n=40) [14]. Results of these registrations were not available in the listings reviewed. Published diabetes trials and reviews are described above. [5][6][2]
